issues.legal_issue: The ground for eviction based on a tenant securing alternative accommodation applies to both residential and non-residential premises.
material_facts: The tenant used the rented premises as a clinic, rather than as a residence.
The tenant had built another, large house and let portions of it to a government department.
The relevant provision referred to a “house,” which the governing order defined to include residential and non-residential buildings.
An explanation addressed a limited situation involving a tenant who owned a residential house constructed on specified kinds of sites; the main provision itself was left unchanged.
issues.conclusion: The ground applies to non-residential as well as residential premises; the explanation does not exclude non-residential premises from its scope.
issues.legal_principle: Under clause 13(3)(v) of the C.P. & Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949, “house” includes a residential or non-residential building. The provision covers two situations—securing alternative accommodation and leaving the area for a continuous period of four months without reasonably needing the house—and does not distinguish between residential and non-residential premises. The explanation creates a limited legal fiction for specified cases involving ownership of a residential house; it clarifies what counts as securing alternative accommodation in those cases but does not displace the wider main provision. The court also rejected reliance on other States’ rent laws, observing that legislative policy differs.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and rented_premises_used_for_nonresidential_purpose and tenant_secured_other_accommodation and main_ground_covers_two_situations and explanation_covers_only_limited_residential_class

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought permission to end a tenancy under a rent-control eviction procedure.
predicates.rented_premises_used_for_nonresidential_: The tenant used the rented premises for a purpose other than residence.
predicates.tenant_secured_other_accommodation: The tenant obtained other accommodation apart from the rented premises.
predicates.main_ground_covers_two_situations: The governing ground covered both obtaining other accommodation and leaving the area without reasonably needing the rented premises.
predicates.explanation_covers_only_limited_resident: An explanation to the governing ground addressed only a limited class of cases involving ownership of a residential house.

issues.definition: When a rent-control eviction proceeding concerns premises used for a non-residential purpose, and the tenant has obtained other accommodation under a ground that covers two situations despite an explanation limited to a residential class, that ground applies to non-residential premises.

issues.legal_issue: The requirement that the tenant not reasonably need the rented premises applies to the leaving-the-area ground, while the concept of alternative accommodation itself requires that the other accommodation reasonably meet the tenant’s needs.
material_facts: The provision set out securing alternative accommodation and leaving the area for a continuous period as separate grounds, followed by the words that the tenant “does not reasonably need the house.”
The courts below had considered whether the other building available to the tenant could reasonably meet his requirements and had recorded findings against him.
issues.conclusion: The words “and does not reasonably need the house” govern the leaving-the-area ground, not the alternative-accommodation ground; however, other accommodation is alternative only if it is capable of reasonably meeting the tenant’s requirements.
issues.legal_principle: The court read the punctuation and structure of clause 13(3)(v) as making the final phrase govern the part concerning leaving the area. It held that “alternative” accommodation inherently must be capable of reasonably meeting the tenant’s requirements. No earlier case was relied on for this interpretation.

predicates.rent_control_interpretation_proceeding: A court had to interpret a ground for eviction in a rent-control proceeding.
predicates.ground_sets_out_two_situations_together: The ground stated obtaining other accommodation and leaving the area as separate situations in the same provision.
predicates.final_need_phrase_follows_second_situati: The words about not reasonably needing the rented premises followed the wording about leaving the area.
predicates.other_accommodation_assessed_for_tenant_: The courts considered whether the other building available to the tenant could reasonably meet his requirements.

issues.definition: When a rent-control ground sets out obtaining accommodation and leaving the area together, places the need phrase after the latter, and the other accommodation is assessed against the tenant’s requirements, the need phrase governs leaving the area while alternative accommodation must reasonably meet those requirements.

issues.legal_issue: Delay in seeking permission to end a tenancy does not defeat the application where later circumstances explain the timing and the delay does not establish waiver.
material_facts: The tenant had built the other house several years before the eviction applications were filed.
After a partition, the landlord applicants became entitled to exclusive possession of their respective portions of the rented premises.
Evidence indicated that the tenant was approaching retirement and was trying to establish his son, also a doctor, in the premises.

The appellant relied on Mansaram v. S. P. Pathak, where the court had found waiver in circumstances involving a long-known alleged illegal occupation, numerous earlier proceedings, and a claim raised after the original landlord’s death by a stranger.
issues.conclusion: The delay argument had no substance: the later partition and the circumstances concerning the tenant’s practice explained the timing, and Mansaram did not support the appellant’s argument.
issues.legal_principle: The court distinguished Mansaram v. S. P. Pathak, [1984] 1 SCC 125, in which the principle of waiver applied because the alleged illegal entry had not been raised over many years and proceedings and was raised after the original landlord’s death by a stranger. Here, the evidence showed later circumstances relevant to the landlords’ entitlement and the tenant’s circumstances. The court did not hold that any action filed within a limitation period is necessarily immune from dismissal for delay.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and alternative_accommodation_predated_application and later_partition_changed_landlords_entitlement and evidence_showed_tenant_nearing_retirement_and_establishing_successor and no_comparable_waiver_circumstances

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord applied for permission to end a tenancy under a rent-control procedure.
predicates.alternative_accommodation_predated_appli: The tenant had obtained other accommodation before the landlord made the eviction application.
predicates.later_partition_changed_landlords_entitl: A later division of ownership gave the applicants exclusive entitlement to the portions occupied by the tenant.
predicates.evidence_showed_tenant_nearing_retiremen: Evidence indicated that the tenant was nearing retirement and seeking to establish a family member in the premises.
predicates.no_comparable_waiver_circumstances: The claim was not one raised after prolonged inaction by a stranger in circumstances comparable to the cited waiver case.

issues.definition: When a rent-control eviction application concerns accommodation obtained earlier, later changes affect the landlords’ entitlement, evidence explains the tenant-related timing, and comparable waiver circumstances are absent, delay does not defeat the application.
